title: Swedish inquiry frames social exclusion as an interaction among segregation, institutional distrust, discrimination, alternative systems and constrained individual rights
source_unit: Government of Sweden, SOU 2026:53 Parallella samhällsstrukturer – ett kunskapsunderlag för förbättrad integration och minskat utanförskap
geography: Sweden; national policy inquiry with attention to local areas, institutions, migrants, children, women and socially excluded communities

denominator.unit: Swedish government inquiry and 610-page final report

composite_problem.value: The inquiry treats ‘parallel social structures’ as a composite problem in which normative systems, power structures, institutional distrust, segregation, social exclusion, discrimination, alternative social systems and sometimes criminality interact.

not_single_group.value: The report explicitly says the phenomenon cannot be understood as one group or as all residents of disadvantaged areas; cultural diversity, religious affiliation and collective organisation remain protected features of an open democracy.

observations.method: Government-commissioned inquiry synthesising research, official knowledge and stakeholder experience; the report develops a working concept rather than a single prevalence estimate.
observations.uncertainty: The inquiry says the term has no generally accepted definition and that the phenomena it combines are difficult to distinguish and measure causally.
observations.subgroup: Groups, local communities and institutions experiencing different combinations of integration, exclusion, trust and rights constraints.
observations.counterinterpretation: The framework may be useful for coordinating policy domains, but its composite character makes it vulnerable to over-broad labeling unless local evidence and individual rights safeguards are maintained.

observations.period: 2026 inquiry; trust, segregation, discrimination and institutional inclusion

denominator.unit: Swedish government inquiry and its cited research base

trust_pattern.value: Sweden is generally characterised by high social trust, but trust varies across groups and tends to be lower among foreign-born people; education, health and employment are associated with higher trust.

institutional_requirement.value: The inquiry calls for public authorities to act lawfully, effectively, impartially and without discrimination, particularly in areas marked by exclusion and low trust.

rights_mechanism.value: It describes segregation and discrimination in housing and labour markets as possible contributors to separation from wider society and constrained access to rights.

observations.method: Synthesis of comparative research, Swedish administrative and policy knowledge, and inquiry analysis; relationships are not estimated as one causal model.
observations.uncertainty: The report notes that trust, segregation, socioeconomic disadvantage and discrimination often co-occur, making it difficult to identify which factor is most important in a given setting.
observations.subgroup: Foreign-born people, residents of segregated or disadvantaged areas, and people encountering housing, labour-market or public-authority barriers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower trust among a group may reflect institutional treatment and exclusion as much as internal norms; the report does not justify treating group identity as a causal explanation by itself.

observations.period: 2026 inquiry; alternative social systems and everyday access to institutions

denominator.unit: Swedish government inquiry and its qualitative evidence base

alternative_routes.value: The report describes informal or alternative routes for conflict resolution, housing allocation, livelihoods, education, information, protection and financial matters.

rights_risk.value: These routes become especially problematic when customary or internal rules displace statutory rights or make it harder for people with weak positions within a group to assert their interests.

institutional_legitimacy.value: Reliance on informal leaders, criminal actors or internal networks can weaken the legitimacy and reach of ordinary public institutions.

observations.method: Conceptual and empirical synthesis in the inquiry; examples are not a national count of all informal activity or evidence that every community using informal support is harmful.
observations.uncertainty: The report distinguishes benign community organisation from systems that restrict fundamental rights, but does not provide a single prevalence measure for each alternative route.
observations.subgroup: Women, children, LGBTI people and others with weaker bargaining power inside restrictive family, customary or network structures, as well as residents who lack accessible formal routes.
observations.counterinterpretation: Informal community support can fill gaps left by inaccessible or distrusted institutions; the key analytic question is whether it expands or restricts individual agency and rights.

observations.period: 2026 inquiry; policy response and intergenerational persistence

measurement_gap.value: The inquiry reports no national overview and no single indicator for prevalence, recommending combined indicators that capture rights constraints, institutional distrust, alternative systems, separation and everyday life.

policy_portfolio.value: Recommended action spans governance and follow-up, integration and gender equality, prevention for children and young people, reducing segregation and strengthening excluded areas, and societal resilience.

intergenerational_risk.value: The report warns that without sustained preventive and promotive efforts, restrictive structures may be reproduced across generations, with schools and preschools serving as important institutional sites.

observations.method: Policy inquiry recommendations based on the report’s multi-domain synthesis; these are proposed routes, not evaluated interventions.
observations.uncertainty: The recommendations do not establish which interventions will improve integration, trust, gender equality or rights in practice, nor how outcomes should be attributed across national, regional and local actors.
observations.subgroup: Children and young people, women, municipalities, schools, public authorities, civil society, businesses, property owners and local communities.
observations.counterinterpretation: A multi-domain policy portfolio can improve coordination, but it can also diffuse accountability unless each intervention has clear authority, measures, safeguards and follow-up.

related_sources.claim: Official English government summary of the inquiry’s framing and five policy areas.
Official Swedish report landing page and publication metadata.

boundary: This record treats SOU 2026:53 as a government inquiry and policy knowledge base, not as a neutral prevalence census or a causal evaluation. Its politically charged term ‘parallel social structures’ has no generally accepted definition; the report itself stresses interaction among exclusion, discrimination, trust, segregation, alternative systems and rights constraints, and warns against equating all cultural, religious or migrant communities with the phenomenon.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official 610-page PDF and government English summary were reviewed, especially the English summary pages 35-49 for definitions, measurement limits, trust, alternative systems, rights boundaries, intergenerational risks and policy recommendations.
